title: Castlevania Turns 40, And Konami May Have Just Teased A 3D Collection
author: Darryn Bonthuys
text:
Castlevania celebrated its 40th anniversary this week--an impressive milestone in video games and a terrifying pair of numbers for anyone who was born in 1987. Konami marked the occasion with a new video paying tribute to the original whip-slinging hero of the 1986 Famicom game, as well as all of the other influential entries in the Castlevania series over the last four decades. It's a cute little retrospective, and it might also be teasing something else from Konami, if our tinfoil-hat-speculation is right.
https://youtu.be/U9hmHw0JFUc
Right near the end of the video, Castlevania's first protagonist, Simon Belmont, takes a quick stroll past a series of non-ruined portraits in Dracula's castle. Eagle-eyed observers will note that these feature cover art from three of the 3D-era games--Lament of Innocence, Curse of Darkness, and Lords of Shadow. The fourth one is for Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, which launches in October 2026. Could Konami be teeing up a new compilation that bundles together the PS2 and Xbox 360/PS3-era 3D Castlevania games?
Portraits of ruin? Nah, just some really good games.
The company isn't saying anything, and there's a good chance that the games were chosen purely because they still have some of the best cover art in the franchise. They're pretty neat, artistically! But a Castlevania collection isn't uncommon, as Konami has released a few of these in the past. The Castlevania Anniversary Collection from 2019 collected eight games spanning the first 10 years of the series, and the Castlevania: Dominus Collection bundled all three DS-era games alongside the 1988 Haunted Castle arcade game.
What Konami did confirm is that it will hold sales for select Castlevania titles, new vinyl record soundtracks for classic games are available to preorder, and Castlevania on mobile is also free for a limited time through the iOS and Android stores.
For Castlevania fans, next month's release of Castlevania: Belmont's Curse marks a major moment for the series. Following the release of Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 in 2014, the video game series went on hiatus, aside from the two compilations released. The Castlevania animated adaptations released for Netflix proved that there was still an appetite for the IP, and last year, it was announced that the developer of The Rogue Prince of Persia--Evil Empire--was reviving castlevania for PC and console.
So far, Belmont's Curse looks like a return to the series' roots, as it follows Rose Belmont through the ruined streets of Paris on her quest to stop Dracula. The game will let you turn tough bosses into powerful allies , and a demo for it will go live on October 1 ahead of its October 15 release date. Beyond that, there's hope that we could see more Castlevania in the future, as Konami's decision to outsource development to studios like Bloober Team and Screen Burn has led to several excellent new entries that have redefined what Silent Hill can be.
It looks like it's repeating this approach with Castlevania, and a compilation of the cult-classic 3D games sandwiched between new releases would be a fun way to kickstart a Castlevania renaissance.
A Pile Of Secrets: The Hidden Gems Of The Castlevania Series

title: 《皇牌空战 8 希孚之翼》多人模式前瞻：短暂但激烈｜IGN 中国
author: Kamui Ye
text:
多人大厅、虚拟形象，终于有了能互动的战友
尽管“多人模式”显然并非第一次出现在《皇牌空战》系列里，十几年前甚至出过一款专门的多人对战游戏《皇牌空战：无限》，但直到即将在 2026 年 10 月 2 日发售的《皇牌空战 8 希孚之翼》中，制作组才首次加入了跨平台联机以及网络大厅、虚拟形象等 MMO 里常见的社交功能，允许玩家使用自定义虚拟形象在基地社交交流后再出击，对于多人玩法来说无疑是一次重大进步。
近日我们提前试玩了本作的多人模式玩法，只不过仅限于线上大厅和几个不同的任务种类，跨平台联机暂时没有体验到，总的来讲功能虽然比较基础，但开发团队还是尽力打造了一个相对便捷的联机环境，通过很简单的手柄操作就能完成包括组队、自定义、休闲在内的一系列准备工作，抛开由于特殊的游戏版本、特定的网络环境导致的一些联机小 Bug 不谈，整个体验过程还是十分顺畅的。
进入多人联机模式之后，首先你会来到一个类似“航空基地”的地方，这里面积并不太大，由一片广场、几座机库以及环绕广场的一些集装箱临时建筑构成，但玩家可以在这里看到自己的虚拟形象、可以自由走动，当然也可以看到被分配至这个基地的其他玩家。
我猜后台系统应该采用了类似“频道大厅”的设计，选择某个地区的服务器之后，角色就会被随机分配到几十、上百个大厅里，每一个大厅最多支持 100 名玩家进入，大家共享一个广场，当然你也可以通过出入口直接前往其他的大厅。
从四周的设施来看，首先必不可少的个人形象设定“Avatar Settings”，在这里可以更换服装、发型等等，但这些道具的获取方式，要么通过完成任务得到奖励，要么直接去“ACE COMBAT STORE”商店通过代币购买。
游戏里一共有 3 种货币，最常见的是内置的普通货币，另外还有“蓝币”和“黄币”，前者的暂定价格为 10 美元兑换 1000 蓝币，不用在游戏里做任务攒钱就能直接买到诸如角色服装、贴图道具以及机体涂装、新机体等内容，可以节约大量时间，不过 DEMO 里暂时没有看到使用黄色代币的场景，推测可能跟更高级的道具有关。
由于多人模式里全都是需要多人联机组队才能接取的任务，所以在跟好友组成一支最大 4 人的队伍之前能做的事情很少，单人的话甚至只能去练习模式看看机体涂装和试试手感，没办法正常参与游戏。
经过开发商的现场组织，我们几位媒体组成了一个临时的 4 人小队，再经过一小段时间的匹配等待，终于正式开始了测试。在等待匹配的时候可以到街机厅游玩一些 NAMCO 的经典街机游戏，包括《吃豆人（PAC-MAN）》《大蜜蜂（GALAGA）》《迷魂车（RALLY-X）》还有《龙魂（DRAGON SPIRIT）》四种。
此次试玩活动提供的多人玩法一共有三种，分别是 CO-OP ASSAULT（PvE）、CO-OP WARFARE（PvPvE） 以及 TEAM DEATHMATCH（PvP），在进行匹配之前所有队伍成员都需要先把自己的任务模式调整到统一的状态之下，不同模式之间无法交叉或随机匹配，完成之后就会进入机体选择画面，也是要等所有人都确定之后才能开始。
虽然现场玩到的都是 4 人组队的任务，不过在测试时我也跟一名玩家意外组成一个 2人小队完成了一个PVE任务，说明正式版中可能存在比较灵活和多样化的任务模式，并不一定非要凑齐 4 个人才会开打。
由于时间限制，三种任务类型我们每种大约测试了 2 次，由于队友和对手战机全都从剧情模式的 AI 换成了真人，导致交流方式显然有了一些变化，战斗难度也是直线上升。
我自己虽然已经很多年不玩《皇牌空战》系列，但本以为凭借早年间积累的好几代游戏数百小时游戏经验，不至于打得太难看，结果上手才发现整个战场气氛跟单机版大相径庭 —— 对手玩家有着十分娴熟的摆脱咬尾技巧，利用机体速度变化缩小回旋半径以规避导弹追踪这类操作也是家常便饭，而新组建的队伍成员相互之间根本谈不上沟通和交流，而这在 PVP 战斗中显然至关重要。
和带着几十上百发空空弹无脑“打火鸡”的故事模式相比，在线多人模式的紧张程度显然上升了不止一个档次，并且也相对而言更贴近真实空战的危险情况。不过根据规则，进入战斗的队伍最终都是凭借分数来判定输赢，所以在有 PVE 元素的任务中，如果有办法躲开人群，挑选一些装备有对地攻击弹药的机体，集中注意力摧毁敌机以外的任务目标，比如地面上的油罐、战车、雷达等设施，除了纯粹捉对厮杀的 TEAM DEATHMATCH 模式以外，理论上也能获得一些分数帮助队伍获胜。
几场联机战斗结束后，首先最大的感受是每局对战的时间都偏短，最短的大概只有 3分钟，最长的一局也就 6 分钟左右，感觉刚刚才开始适应战场的气氛就直接跳出任务了，有种意犹未尽的感觉（虽说基本上一直在挨打）。
其次哪怕选了比较皮实的机体，但面对真人玩家的猛烈进攻也没太大意义，归根结底还是要苦练操作本领才行，故事模式下的一些交战经验、规则在组队联机模式里基本都不再适用，时刻保持神经紧绷以及娴熟的操作才是获取高分的终极保障。
当然，如果能找到固定的队友开着麦一边沟通一边作战，显然比单打独斗要好很多，就像现实中的战斗机也基本没有单机出任务的一样，长机僚机相互掩护、勾引是最基本的空战战术，在《皇牌空战 8 希孚之翼》里终于有希望更好地实现这种贴近现实的战斗氛围了。

title: 本周 Steam 值得关注的游戏 09.21 - 09.27（五）
author: 游戏发现
text:
第四部分
注： 本系列文章的信息主要整合自 Steam 与 SteamDB 的即将发售列表，由于 Steam 支持手动输入日期及发售、同步不及时等原因，本列表可能会遗漏收录一些作品的发售信息。如果本周有您的作品或您喜欢的作品未被列出，欢迎直接评论补充链接～～
HIROTONFA’s American Revolution Smuggler
关键字： 模拟、贸易、角色扮演、管理
发行日期： 2026/09/25（暂无中文）EA
与一个州谈恋爱吧！在这款混乱的美国革命商贸模拟游戏中，低买高卖，躲避英国皇家海军和爱国者私掠船，并与殖民地各州的州长们展开浪漫恋情。重商主义万岁！
Substrate: Emergence
关键字： 沙盒、模拟、生物收集
发行日期： 2026/09/25（暂无中文）EA
在培养皿竞技场中培育荧光细胞群落，这些细胞会发生突变、成群结队并相互吞噬。在这款细节丰富的人工生命模拟游戏中，与竞争对手实验室一较高下，培育出属于你自己的独特生物体系。
FRUKT
关键字： 鲜血、暴力、沙盒、物理
发行日期： 2026/09/25（暂无中文）EA
一款基于体素的死亡沙盒游戏。利用逼真的身体物理效果，射击、肢解并碾压 NPC。
Farming Camp
关键字： 农场模拟、互动小说、休闲
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）
每年夏天，恒树农业营都会寻找下一任最优秀的恒树农夫，此人会把农业拉高到新的水平。年轻的亚历山德拉怀揣着对美好未来的憧憬而参赛，力争夺得冠军。但她必须面对同龄人的较量，并探索成为恒树农夫的意义。
EA SPORTS FC™ 27
关键字： 体育、足球、多人
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）
欢迎在《EA SPORTS FC™ 27》中体验全世界的游戏。 踏入 The Grounds，体验这座连接街头与球场的足球乐园；随着灵感源自社区反馈的创新带来更真实的足球玩法，在每一种模式中感受更强的掌控力。
光陨之地（Land of Glarefall）
关键字： 动作角色扮演、塔防、生存
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）
《光陨之地》是一款角色动作冒险和策略生存为核心玩法的游戏，且融合了地图自由探索与资源管理机制。玩家将扮演王国调查团的一员，随着剧情深入，逐步揭开“黑金”与魔物的真相。
Tank Battle Classic
关键字： 战争游戏、坦克、车辆作战、二战
发行日期： 2026/09/25（暂无中文）
一款采用复古风格画面的坦克战斗动作游戏，以二战坦克为特色，提供单人战斗模式。
魔法之境（Magic Realm）
关键字： 打砖块、轻度 Rogue、视觉小说
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）
《魔法之境》是一款充满奇幻与冒险的叙事驱动的打砖块肉鸽游戏。 玩家将扮演年轻的魔法师西斯塔亚，与好友荧惑一同在神秘的魔法世界中探索未知的领域。为了实现共同的梦想，你们将踏入充满危险的迷雾森林，揭开古堡中隐藏的古老魔法秘密。游戏融合了魔法战斗、药水系统和艰难的抉择，玩家将面对魔物、神秘的魔法物品以及隐藏在背后的阴谋。通过智慧和勇气，你将决定故事的走向，带领伙伴们走向光明的未来。准备好迎接这场充满魔法与挑战的冒险了吗?
猫愿日记（Neko Diary🐾）
关键字： 视觉小说、恋爱模拟
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）
🐾 埋藏在幼猫心中的小小愿望，是否能传达到呢？这是仅有一室、一人、一猫娘的一场温馨且治愈的同居故事。让猫娘用恋慕之心温暖您的冬天！
Sector 13: Haunted Woods
关键字： 心理恐怖、在线合作、冒险、突发惊吓
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）
《13 号区：诅咒之林》是一款支持 1-4 人联机的开放世界恐怖生存游戏。你的目标是在这片充满未知的土地上寻找异象 (Anomalies)。 探索神秘区域，回收禁忌文物，并在阴森的森林中生存下来。请务必小心——你的麦克风可能会暴露你的位置导致死亡，但也可能是你和队友击退步步逼近的敌人的唯一武器。💀
西部拓荒纪（Wild West Pioneers）
关键字： 城市营造、模拟、策略
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）EA
《西部拓荒纪》是一款城市建造冒险游戏，你将带领一群拓荒者深入尚未开垦的西部边疆。建设并管理不断发展的聚落，建立完整的生产链，探索广袤世界，并亲历一段关于淘金梦想、危险遭遇与寻找家人的西部故事。
Black Cat Book Club
关键字： 桌面伴侣、挂机游戏、猫
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）
一个你可以放在桌面上的魔法图书馆。在这款温馨的放置游戏中，帮助黑猫研究古老的典籍并学习魔法。
Cielle is Not Happy
关键字： 冒险、角色扮演、视觉小说、心理恐怖
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）
《Cielle is Not Happy》是一款心理恐怖角色扮演游戏，通过深刻而令人心神不宁的剧情以及别出心裁的战斗机制，重新定义了冒险游戏这一类型，为玩家带来极具沉浸感的游戏体验。
Lunar Drifter
关键字： 第一人称射击、街机、快节奏
发行日期： 2026/09/25（暂无中文）

关键字： 农场管理、龙、模拟
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）

Heisenberg 101
关键字： 解谜、推箱子、逻辑
发行日期： 2026/09/25（暂无中文）

关键字： 推箱子、解谜

Sockpuppet Noir
关键字： 推理、视觉小说、黑色幽默
发行日期： 2026/09/25（暂无中文）

复生之泪：泛山行（Tears of Vanfell）
关键字： 动作类 Rogue、砍杀
发行日期： 2026/09/25（ 中文支持 ）

Archipeo
关键字： 城市营造、模拟、资源管理

Sandwich +1
关键字： 增量、烹饪、短篇

Lucid Cats

注：本系列文章的信息主要整合自 Steam 与 SteamDB 的即将发售列表，由于 Steam 支持手动输入日期及发售、同步不及时等原因，本列表可能会遗漏收录一些作品的发售信息。如果本周有您的作品或您喜欢的作品未被列出，欢迎直接评论补充链接～～

HIROTONFA’s American Revolution Smuggler

关键字：模拟、贸易、角色扮演、管理

发行日期：2026/09/25（暂无中文）EA

与一个州谈恋爱吧！在这款混乱的美国革命商贸模拟游戏中，低买高卖，躲避英国皇家海军和爱国者私掠船，并与殖民地各州的州长们展开浪漫恋情。重商主义万岁！

Substrate: Emergence

关键字：沙盒、模拟、生物收集

发行日期：2026/09/25（暂无中文）EA

在培养皿竞技场中培育荧光细胞群落，这些细胞会发生突变、成群结队并相互吞噬。在这款细节丰富的人工生命模拟游戏中，与竞争对手实验室一较高下，培育出属于你自己的独特生物体系。

FRUKT

关键字：鲜血、暴力、沙盒、物理

发行日期：2026/09/25（暂无中文）EA

一款基于体素的死亡沙盒游戏。利用逼真的身体物理效果，射击、肢解并碾压 NPC。

Farming Camp

关键字：农场模拟、互动小说、休闲

发行日期：2026/09/25（中文支持）

每年夏天，恒树农业营都会寻找下一任最优秀的恒树农夫，此人会把农业拉高到新的水平。年轻的亚历山德拉怀揣着对美好未来的憧憬而参赛，力争夺得冠军。但她必须面对同龄人的较量，并探索成为恒树农夫的意义。

EA SPORTS FC™ 27

关键字：体育、足球、多人

发行日期：2026/09/25（中文支持）

欢迎在《EA SPORTS FC™ 27》中体验全世界的游戏。 踏入 The Grounds，体验这座连接街头与球场的足球乐园；随着灵感源自社区反馈的创新带来更真实的足球玩法，在每一种模式中感受更强的掌控力。

光陨之地（Land of Glarefall）

关键字：动作角色扮演、塔防、生存

发行日期：2026/09/25（中文支持）

《光陨之地》是一款角色动作冒险和策略生存为核心玩法的游戏，且融合了地图自由探索与资源管理机制。玩家将扮演王国调查团的一员，随着剧情深入，逐步揭开“黑金”与魔物的真相。

Tank Battle Classic

关键字：战争游戏、坦克、车辆作战、二战

发行日期：2026/09/25（暂无中文）

一款采用复古风格画面的坦克战斗动作游戏，以二战坦克为特色，提供单人战斗模式。

魔法之境（Magic Realm）

关键字：打砖块、轻度 Rogue、视觉小说

发行日期：2026/09/25（中文支持）

《魔法之境》是一款充满奇幻与冒险的叙事驱动的打砖块肉鸽游戏。 玩家将扮演年轻的魔法师西斯塔亚，与好友荧惑一同在神秘的魔法世界中探索未知的领域。为了实现共同的梦想，你们将踏入充满危险的迷雾森林，揭开古堡中隐藏的古老魔法秘密。游戏融合了魔法战斗、药水系统和艰难的抉择，玩家将面对魔物、神秘的魔法物品以及隐藏在背后的阴谋。通过智慧和勇气，你将决定故事的走向，带领伙伴们走向光明的未来。准备好迎接这场充满魔法与挑战的冒险了吗?

猫愿日记（Neko Diary🐾）

关键字：视觉小说、恋爱模拟

发行日期：2026/09/25（中文支持）

🐾 埋藏在幼猫心中的小小愿望，是否能传达到呢？这是仅有一室、一人、一猫娘的一场温馨且治愈的同居故事。让猫娘用恋慕之心温暖您的冬天！

Sector 13: Haunted Woods

关键字：心理恐怖、在线合作、冒险、突发惊吓

发行日期：2026/09/25（中文支持）

关键字：城市营造、模拟、策略

发行日期：2026/09/25（中文支持）EA

Black Cat Book Club

关键字：桌面伴侣、挂机游戏、猫

title: Oh, the places you'll game: Aerospace engineers use Steam Deck to steer Mars rover prototype
author: Jess Kinghorn
text:
Here's one for you: Let's say you're a scientist tasked with designing an intuitive physical interface for a human operator to remotely control a robot destined to rove Mars. What do you do? Well, it turns out there's no need to reinvent the wheel.
Airbus recently showed off its ExoMars rover to documentarian Tom Scott , even letting him have a go at steering it. The remote control device the aerospace company uses turns out to be a modified Steam Deck . Whether it's the LCD or OLED model, I can't say but it looks like the standard version to me.
During the short documentary, the rover is driven forward via the handheld gaming PC. A 'bumper' press then turns the wheels around 90-degrees, avoiding the need for an awkward turning circle or the possibility of getting stuck on a space rock.
The team at the aerospace company's Stevenage campus in the UK are developing autonomous navigation for the ExoMars rover, using what appears to be custom software running from a Steam Deck to navigate the terrain of their test bed. When the rover finally touches down on the Red Planet, it won't need to be steered via Valve's handheld.
The company is aiming to send a rover called the Rosalind Franklin to Mars in 2030, with the whole project described as " the culmination of more than 20 years’ work ," by Airbus Defence and Space UK managing director Kata Escott (via Tom's Hardware ). In addition to autonomous navigation, the company is also developing the rover landing platform's mechanical, thermal and propulsion systems.
There'll be no gamer den on that Mars landing platform, but it's still neat that Valve's handheld was a stepping stone on the journey there. And they say videogames can't teach you anything…

title: I cannot believe this obscure MMO from my childhood is still going 23 years later
author: Mollie Taylor
text:
I grew up in the 2000s with a PC but not a whole lot of money. That's the kind of combination that gets you bargain-bin Sold Out Software games from Poundland or, more so in my case, an absurd number of free-to-play online and browser-based games that were utterly pervasive across the internet.
My childhood was a never-ending revolving door of these mid-tier Flash and Java games. Some have long left my memory, a fleeting experience. But some continue to rattle around in my brain, reminding me of simpler times where I didn't have to pay taxes or subject myself to at least one hour of screen-free time before bed lest I wake up with a headache the next morning.
But where are these weird and wonderful games now? Are they still scattered across the internet? Are they in their original forms, practically untouched, or have they evolved into far deeper and darker games than they once were?
Well, as I continue to march into my 30s against my will, I've been thinking back to the games I would play as a child and asking myself just that question. So why don't we go and check in on a couple of them?
Where the hell is Puzzle Pirates now?
Puzzle Pirates is, if you haven't already guessed, an MMO where you are a pirate and you do puzzles. Every component of a ship's operation is done through different puzzles—bilging is a Bejeweled-inspired match three, sailing is a buccaneering Doctor Mario, patching the sails is incredibly similar to Pipe Dream. You get the drill.
(Image credit: Grey Havens) It's an incredible niche premise, one I expected to have long sunk. Except… it hasn't? As I popped on the internet to see if the game was still kicking around, I was shocked to discover that it was. Hell, it's on Steam. Still official and everything! No private, fan-run server to be seen! A couple seconds and a mere 85mb download later and my ears were being thoroughly blasted with jaunty pirate tunes. A search through my ancient childhood email inbox revealed that my original account was unfortunately deleted in 2012, so I made a brand-new pirate called Johnpcgamer (pirates are a singular-named folk, it seems) and dove right in.
And, well, aside from being told how to purchase premium currency within the first 60 seconds of being born, it's exactly how I remembered it. There are a lot less mateys milling around these days—most of them seemed to be the real for-lifers, ones with more trophies and gold and puzzle proficiency than most of the server combines—so I dove into a few tutorial voyages with some friendly bot pirates.
As a child I mostly stuck to bilging—as far as I could remember it was one of the easiest, and it was also one of the main duties assigned to scrubs like myself. I made a start with that one, before moving on to carpentry and rigging. And the minigames still hold up surprisingly well today, unsurprising considering most of them are inspired by iconic, already-established puzzles.
(Image credit: Grey Havens) The occasional mid-voyage reports were informing me that I was, unfortunately, doing a little bit shit. The puzzles are good, but they require a level of speed, foresight, and cleverness that I clearly do not possess. At least there were no real-player captains there to yell at me about it.
After sailing the high seas for a little while, I went for a quick stroll around the town of the island my ship had arrived at. It was stuffed to the brim with tailors—every business in Puzzle Pirates is player-owned, and as with all MMOs I assume fashion is the endgame—with a single inn wedged between them all.
I nipped in, hoping to partake in drinking games with some NPCs. Unfortunately, they all massively outclassed me and in a display of pirate honour, politely refused to go toe-to-toe with me in a drinking contest lest I end up in some sort of hydrogen bomb vs coughing baby scenario.
(Image credit: Grey Havens) Unfortunately, much of Puzzle Pirates seems to be gated off to swabs like me. Everything is too expensive (even buying doubloons, the game's premium currency), a good handful of the minigames are paywalled behind a subscription, along with many of its systems. But that's exactly how I remember it, so I'm taking a weird sort of comfort in this deja vu.
It's strange seeing this relic of my childhood stand the test of time. A niche MMO that I'd be surprised if it was drawing even triple-digit numbers these days, still drifting along the ocean slowly but surely. I doubt I'll be going back anytime soon, but I'm happy I even have the option to in the first place.

As a child I mostly stuck to bilging—as far as I could remember it was one of the easiest, and it was also one of the main duties assigned to scrubs like myself. I made a start with that one, before moving on to carpentry and rigging. And the minigames still hold up surprisingly well today, unsurprising considering most of them are inspired by iconic, already-established puzzles.

The occasional mid-voyage reports were informing me that I was, unfortunately, doing a little bit shit. The puzzles are good, but they require a level of speed, foresight, and cleverness that I clearly do not possess. At least there were no real-player captains there to yell at me about it.

After sailing the high seas for a little while, I went for a quick stroll around the town of the island my ship had arrived at. It was stuffed to the brim with tailors—every business in Puzzle Pirates is player-owned, and as with all MMOs I assume fashion is the endgame—with a single inn wedged between them all.

I nipped in, hoping to partake in drinking games with some NPCs. Unfortunately, they all massively outclassed me and in a display of pirate honour, politely refused to go toe-to-toe with me in a drinking contest lest I end up in some sort of hydrogen bomb vs coughing baby scenario.

Unfortunately, much of Puzzle Pirates seems to be gated off to swabs like me. Everything is too expensive (even buying doubloons, the game's premium currency), a good handful of the minigames are paywalled behind a subscription, along with many of its systems. But that's exactly how I remember it, so I'm taking a weird sort of comfort in this deja vu.

It's strange seeing this relic of my childhood stand the test of time. A niche MMO that I'd be surprised if it was drawing even triple-digit numbers these days, still drifting along the ocean slowly but surely. I doubt I'll be going back anytime soon, but I'm happy I even have the option to in the first place.

title: My greatest GTA 5 challenge yet: Random teleports every 50 seconds
author: Joshua Wolens
text:
Los Santos Customs
I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier .
It's the greatest challenge I've yet faced. Not in Grand Theft Auto 5, in life (I was a sheltered child). Forget hit squads, forget running a billion-dollar privacy-invading company, forget bad credit, forget the absence of gravity. My enemy now is space itself, the third dimension. Maybe spacetime. Never been clear on what that is.
I have installed the Random Teleport Challenge , which is not a challenge in the American Gladiators sense but more of a challenge in the debilitating disease sense. Every 50 seconds, the game whisks me to one of 28 locations scattered across GTA 5's map. I have no list of which locations these are, which makes the whole thing quite exciting.
I don't know how you live your life, but for me, it's actually quite disruptive to find myself randomly spatially displaced every 50 seconds. It's probably how the Quantum Leap guy felt, if he sometimes Quantum Leapt underneath a truck.
It's a confusing and disconcerting time. Utterly impossible to plan for. But you know what? It taught me an important lesson, probably. Not sure what it is yet, but this seems like one of those things people turn around at the end of and say they learnt an important lesson, so there must be one in there somewhere.
This is my life now. (Image credit: Rockstar) This will probably make it quite difficult to experience mods going forward. I may have to edit an .ini file. Or maybe I just live like this now, ever jaunting. Ever lost in the creases of the sheets of the universe. Just check under the nearest truck; I'm probably there.

title: 'We all thought we were bringing extraction to the masses, and we didn't'
author: Morgan Park
text:
A few illustrative quotes from the "Future of Marathon Part 1" video that Bungie published today. The team (recently reduced by Sony layoffs ) were candid in their plans to transform Marathon from purely an extraction shooter to something more Destiny-shaped: Easier onboarding, dedicated PvE options, a wider variety of PvP (Including a team deathmatch mode), and a greater emphasis on story. This upcoming vision for Marathon sounds less hardcore and, ideally, more broad in its appeal.
The two major milestones for Marathon's future will be the December Symbiosis update and a March 2027 update. Here's what Bungie's laid out for those:
The next 6 months of Marathon
December: Symbiosis introduces Marathon’s first permanent PvE experience, an expanded Perimeter, a new shell, improved onboarding, and a social space.

title: PC Gamer's Hyperfeed beta is live
author: Evan Lahti
text:
Mind our dust! And don't let any of it get into your PC's fans.
We're temporarily testing a new version of the PC Gamer homepage called the Hyperfeed that you'll see getting lots of updates over at pcgamer.com/hyperfeed . This is a very early, pre-pre-proto-alpha test, a minimum-viable version for early data gathering and experimentation. You'll notice a bug or three as we continue to iterate.
Why are we trying something new? The impact of Google's coercive integration of AI has affected the online publishing ecosystem a lot, and we're trying to make our homepage (already the most-visited page on PC Gamer) a much richer experience. We're excited to modernize pcgamer.com in a way that better reflects how you and we play.
Apart from a different look, the main thing you'll notice are short, ephemeral posts currently only found on the Hyperfeed. Gaming in 2026 is so often about the microscopic stuff: character abilities, individual voice lines, a fun character you cooked up in an RPG, two minutes of one session you had in ARC Raiders, a weird ice-poison wand you looted in Diablo 4. We want to talk about our observations and feelings on these small-but-significant things by giving ourselves more flexibility to publish timely, authentic coverage directly from our editors and writers that isn't strictly article-shaped.
Right now in the Hyperfeed, you'll find stuff like this—experiences, gripes, daydreams, and scorpion-related experiences about PC games and hardware such as:
Fraser spending too much money on a spaceship
Jess cramming anime figures into her PC (for science)
Andrea spots a forming supercell of recent tornado games
The upsetting-but-funny things that happened to my simulated alien babies
Ted asks a hard question: "Have you ever actually tried crouch walking?"
Lincoln wishing for a Xavier's School for Gifted Youngsters management sim
We also want to use these short posts to help us quickly react in a timely fashion to serious moments, emerging trends, things devs say, patch notes, and more. Obviously we'll continue to publish loads of daily, in-depth article coverage—this is just another tool that expands our constellation of work.
What's live right now is v0.01, far from the final form of the Hyperfeed, and we have about three-thousand more ideas that haven't been implemented yet, but we'd still like to hear your initial reaction to what you see there, if you have 30 seconds for a short survey .

title: Control Resonant embarrasses me, specifically, with a launch day hotfix negating my main review complaint
author: Lincoln Carpenter
text:
Today is Control Resonant's launch day, and as I wrote in our review , it's peak Remedy. It's a gorgeously surreal atmosphere to sink into—but I had one main complaint. Its combat system centers around building ways to turn your piddly attacks into heavy hitters, which has the unfortunate side effect of making most of its hours of monster fighting a slog of inflated health pools.
Or at least, that was the case until earlier today. Ahead of launch, Remedy released a launch day hotfix that essentially looked me in the eye to say, Nice review you wrote there—would be a real shame if someone made it irrelevant.
(Image credit: Remedy Entertainment) In a Steam news post explaining its changes, Remedy said it's been "keeping a close eye" on player feedback, and based on early responses has juiced protagonist Dylan Faden's combat performance to cut down on the game's pervasive damage sponginess.
"Based on what we have seen so far, we have decided to deploy a hotfix (1.3.3) at launch to address a few specific things: enemy health pools feeling too high, requiring too many hits to Falter (stun) enemies for executions, and Dylan’s overall combat strength early on in the game not feeling powerful enough (even if the man just woke up from a coma)," Remedy said. "We strongly believe these changes will improve the gameplay feel and flow while still providing a challenge."
In other words, Remedy took what I advised in the review—that players should use the in-game Assist Mode settings to spare themselves collective hours of chipping away at health bars by boosting Dylan's outgoing damage and Falter buildup—and made it the default experience.
(Image credit: Remedy Entertainment) And that's fine! It's fine. It'll be a better time for everyone else. It's just that I fought a lot of things during those 30 hours of my life. That's all. But I'm fine!
Remedy also made sure to note that, if you still want to do more fiddling with flow of shapeshifting weapons and boulder-throwing, there's a suite of granular Assist Mode options like enemy aggression adjustments and ability recovery rates for fine-tuning your play experience. If you want, you can even turn Dylan invulnerable and basically set combat to "no." If that sounds appealing, go with God. I won't judge. It's not like it's your job to know.
And if it was someone's job, I'm sure they'd be acting very normal about it.
Control Resonant is available now on Steam .

title: Arc Raiders is finally testing a PvE-only mode: 'We can’t ignore what the data is telling us'
author: Morgan Park
text:
Arc Raiders PvE Test
"To make a long story short, we’re going to be running a test with a PvE matchmaking toggle. This is how it will work:
The test will run from October 13-20, 2026 .
During the test, you will be able to toggle between the classic Arc Raiders PvPvE experience and the PvE experience.
In the PvE experience there will be zero player-to-player damage, and the session is purely focused on the ARC threat and co-op social dynamics.
PvE sessions will include Solos, Duos and Trios in the same session.
We’re designing the system for seamless switching, play PvE for a relaxed solo session then switch back to PvPvE for a high tension match.
Some major conditions, Night Raids, Hidden Bunker, Locked Gate and Frigate will be excluded from the PvE matchmaking test. These are designed with higher tension in mind and rely on the uncertainty of encountering a variety of players.
Your PvPvE matchmaking rating will not be affected while playing in PvE sessions.
It’s important to remember that this is, at least initially, a limited test. When the test ends, the toggle will be removed and matchmaking will return to normal. Your feedback and data will help to shape the future of this system."
(Via Arc Raiders blog )
Despite hesitation, Embark is finally giving a purely PvE version of Arc Raiders a try. It's interesting how they're approaching it as a toggle: Essentially all else about the match will be the same, except that players can't damage each other. Loot will be slightly less valuable than PvPvE sessions to account for the lower risk taken.
Embark has been open about its belief that Arc Raiders' PvP is integral to the experience, but this PvE test exists to "respect that our players have different needs than what we first envisioned." There is no guarantee that anything permanent will come of the test, or that future PvE modes will resemble this toggle.
"We have to respect that some players want to enjoy the game in their own way, and we can’t ignore what the data is telling us," the blog says.
The data Embark is referring to is pretty fascinating if you've followed Arc Raiders' unique community split between friendly and hostile players .
The Arc Raiders population split, according to Embark:
37% Friendly co-op players (this player group has grown consistently since launch).
27% Mixed players.
34% Pure PvP players (this player group has remained stable since launch).
Over 70% of Friendly players and even 40% of PvP players express a desire for fewer hostile encounters and 51% of the surveyed playerbase has expressed an interest in a dedicated PvE option.
There are clear friction points, with friendly players often attempting to avoid PvP entirely, and we hear frustration from certain groups of players around ratting and camping.

title: After mainlining 30 hours of 1440p Bloodborne, I know in my heart it belongs on PC
author: Ted Litchfield
text:
I decided to finally take fate into my own hands. Bloodborne is one of my favorite games of all time, and it is the only one I have spent a significant amount of time playing on the Sony PlayStation 4. I resent that. I hate that horrible little box under my TV with a passion. I think it's only good for watching Gilmore Girls⁠—I don't like playing videogames on it. I am a PC man through and through.
Enter the shadPS4 emulator and BB Launcher , two wonderful tools for running this wonderful game on PC. I followed YouTuber Retro Renew 's guide to emulating Bloodborne, and we were off to the races.
Blood boy
Sekiro, Elden Ring, and Armored Core 6 are all-timer games for me. Crucially, they've demonstrated continued growth and a willingness to experiment on the part of FromSoftware. I don't think the studio "peaked" with Bloodborne by any means, or that its best days are behind it, but there is nothing else out there like it.
The atmosphere and aesthetics of Yharnam are still so striking and odd, like if Nosferatu (pick your version) and Lovecraft were chopped and screwed into black metal album art. It applies the surreal, mythic sensibility of FromSoftware to the modern world, resulting in the most dreamlike, alienating narrative the studio has yet created.
The Healing Church and Byrgenwerth are simultaneously ancient and right there . Master Willem, the primeval progenitor of Cthulhu Studies in this world, is still chilling in a rocking chair on his front porch. Byrgenwerth, a distinctly modern-feeling Cthulhu University, predates the Healing Church. There's this feeling Yharnam regressed from science and study into religious dogmatism, clad in modernity and enlightenment the entire time. But the scientists who created this sickened modernity are hardly blameless, no matter their intentions. Does this remind you of anything?
One reading I had never heard before tuning into the recent Chapo Trap House Players Club episode about Bloodborne is that it's a game about motherhood and mothers, and men ruining the world by doing terrible things to them. It seems so obvious to me now. Kos and her orphan, Queen Yharnam and her child Mergo: The crimes committed against these mothers are the inciting events of the story. You can do the same to Ariana and her child, in the hopes of becoming a god.
God the combat . I fought Ludwig the Accursed earlier than I ever have this playthrough, and it taxed me like little else I've played recently⁠—I felt weirdly shaken afterward. While this is the smallest arsenal of the post-Demon's Souls FromSoft catalogue, every weapon is fully distinct from one another⁠—with the exception of one baffling, fighting game-style moveset clone . Nobody playing Elden Ring would go to the mat for the Highland Axe or Torchpole , but every weapon in Bloodborne has at least one freak out there who will say it's their favorite⁠—I'm a Chikage / Saw Cleaver man, myself.
(Image credit: FromSoftware) Madman's Escort
Bloodborne emulation has been better than the original console experience for some time, but it's still slightly janky. I find "unpatched multiplatform Unreal Engine 5 triple-A port" to be a good comparison point: Basically, the hitches and glitches reminded me of playing Jedi Survivor.
You'll need a beefier rig than for other PS4-era games, and it isn't like there are minimum and recommended specs online anywhere. But I've been surprised at the GPUs I've seen people running Bloodborne on, with one Reddit commenter claiming it was playable on a GTX 1650. I don't have a way of testing, but my wager would be that the RTX 3070 (or equivalent) is the point where you could start expecting reliable 1080p 60fps gameplay.
Digital Foundry demonstrated 4k 60fps gameplay on an RTX 4080 earlier this year, while I've had a pleasant experience at 1440p 60 on an RX 9070 XT from AMD. There's only one glitch that has really spat in my coffee, and I don't have a fix. I've run into two loading zones⁠—the entrance to Yharnam's Grand Cathedral and the elevator depot shortcut in the Forbidden Woods⁠—where, seven out of 10 times, stepping through a doorway turns my field of view into a neon nightmare until I quit and reload.
(Image credit: FromSoftware) Reader, I have tried nearly everything to troubleshoot: Tweaking resolution, VRAM use, shadPS4 versions, lighting settings, FSR use, the gamut. I don't know if it's a Bloodborne on PC thing, or a fromsoftserve BB Remaster mod thing. The only option left is doing a full reinstall, and that just doesn't feel worth the effort for this edge case annoyance. I simply choose to accept it as a quirky old friend now, like having to slam the dashboard of an old car just so to get it to run.
Poison Chalice
I have always refused to be the kind of sucker who pays Sony to let me use the internet I already pay for (the PlayStation Network), so I never really interacted with Bloodborne's online-only procedurally generated dungeons. The PC BB Launcher has a function to force-add procgen dungeons to your save file, and comes with a library of popular ones for loot/experience farming.
I didn't even realize there was a whole sequence of story-based, set Chalice dungeons to explore prior to now⁠—it's possibly FromSoftware's least intuitive, most poorly explained system in any of its games, putting Demon's Souls world tendency to shame.

Free Bloodborne

Sony has largely turned its back on PC gaming after a brief, early 2020s dalliance, and it also recently put down remaster studio Bluepoint for no good reason. While that has spared us from anything like the Demon's Souls Remake being inflicted on Bloodborne, the commonsense, light touch PC port it should have received at any point in the last decade has never felt further away—even though Miyazaki himself told us he isn't against the idea .

html:
I decided to finally take fate into my own hands. Bloodborne is one of my favorite games of all time, and it is the only one I have spent a significant amount of time playing on the Sony PlayStation 4. I resent that. I hate that horrible little box under my TV with a passion. I think it's only good for watching Gilmore Girls⁠—I don't like playing videogames on it. I am a PC man through and through.

Enter the shadPS4 emulator and BB Launcher, two wonderful tools for running this wonderful game on PC. I followed YouTuber Retro Renew's guide to emulating Bloodborne, and we were off to the races.

Blood boy

Sekiro, Elden Ring, and Armored Core 6 are all-timer games for me. Crucially, they've demonstrated continued growth and a willingness to experiment on the part of FromSoftware. I don't think the studio "peaked" with Bloodborne by any means, or that its best days are behind it, but there is nothing else out there like it.

The atmosphere and aesthetics of Yharnam are still so striking and odd, like if Nosferatu (pick your version) and Lovecraft were chopped and screwed into black metal album art. It applies the surreal, mythic sensibility of FromSoftware to the modern world, resulting in the most dreamlike, alienating narrative the studio has yet created.

The Healing Church and Byrgenwerth are simultaneously ancient and right there. Master Willem, the primeval progenitor of Cthulhu Studies in this world, is still chilling in a rocking chair on his front porch. Byrgenwerth, a distinctly modern-feeling Cthulhu University, predates the Healing Church. There's this feeling Yharnam regressed from science and study into religious dogmatism, clad in modernity and enlightenment the entire time. But the scientists who created this sickened modernity are hardly blameless, no matter their intentions. Does this remind you of anything?

One reading I had never heard before tuning into the recent Chapo Trap House Players Club episode about Bloodborne is that it's a game about motherhood and mothers, and men ruining the world by doing terrible things to them. It seems so obvious to me now. Kos and her orphan, Queen Yharnam and her child Mergo: The crimes committed against these mothers are the inciting events of the story. You can do the same to Ariana and her child, in the hopes of becoming a god.

God the combat. I fought Ludwig the Accursed earlier than I ever have this playthrough, and it taxed me like little else I've played recently⁠—I felt weirdly shaken afterward. While this is the smallest arsenal of the post-Demon's Souls FromSoft catalogue, every weapon is fully distinct from one another⁠—with the exception of one baffling, fighting game-style moveset clone. Nobody playing Elden Ring would go to the mat for the Highland Axe or Torchpole, but every weapon in Bloodborne has at least one freak out there who will say it's their favorite⁠—I'm a Chikage/Saw Cleaver man, myself.

Madman's Escort

Bloodborne emulation has been better than the original console experience for some time, but it's still slightly janky. I find "unpatched multiplatform Unreal Engine 5 triple-A port" to be a good comparison point: Basically, the hitches and glitches reminded me of playing Jedi Survivor.

You'll need a beefier rig than for other PS4-era games, and it isn't like there are minimum and recommended specs online anywhere. But I've been surprised at the GPUs I've seen people running Bloodborne on, with one Reddit commenter claiming it was playable on a GTX 1650. I don't have a way of testing, but my wager would be that the RTX 3070 (or equivalent) is the point where you could start expecting reliable 1080p 60fps gameplay.

Digital Foundry demonstrated 4k 60fps gameplay on an RTX 4080 earlier this year, while I've had a pleasant experience at 1440p 60 on an RX 9070 XT from AMD. There's only one glitch that has really spat in my coffee, and I don't have a fix. I've run into two loading zones⁠—the entrance to Yharnam's Grand Cathedral and the elevator depot shortcut in the Forbidden Woods⁠—where, seven out of 10 times, stepping through a doorway turns my field of view into a neon nightmare until I quit and reload.

Reader, I have tried nearly everything to troubleshoot: Tweaking resolution, VRAM use, shadPS4 versions, lighting settings, FSR use, the gamut. I don't know if it's a Bloodborne on PC thing, or a fromsoftserve BB Remaster mod thing. The only option left is doing a full reinstall, and that just doesn't feel worth the effort for this edge case annoyance. I simply choose to accept it as a quirky old friend now, like having to slam the dashboard of an old car just so to get it to run.

Poison Chalice

I have always refused to be the kind of sucker who pays Sony to let me use the internet I already pay for (the PlayStation Network), so I never really interacted with Bloodborne's online-only procedurally generated dungeons. The PC BB Launcher has a function to force-add procgen dungeons to your save file, and comes with a library of popular ones for loot/experience farming.

I didn't even realize there was a whole sequence of story-based, set Chalice dungeons to explore prior to now⁠—it's possibly FromSoftware's least intuitive, most poorly explained system in any of its games, putting Demon's Souls world tendency to shame.

I'm conflicted: This is an astounding bit of nontraditional, asynchronous, and ephemeral online game design like nothing else out there. Swapping tips about choice dungeons on forums and the collective mapping out of optimal seeds is the sort of schoolyard rumor, collective discovery experience FromSoftware is so good at cultivating. I'm sorry I missed it in 2015. But they also really muck up what is otherwise one of the tightest itemization and upgrade systems FromSoftware has ever made.

I got a little bit hooked on some of the more difficult dungeons, and have grinded out the most powerful character I've yet made in Bloodborne⁠. I'm worried the final story areas will be a little too easy with all these extra levels. But hey: At least it's more Bloodborne.

Free Bloodborne

You can play Bloodborne on PC right now, and I recommend the experience. It's a difficult ask for a layman (much less a normie), and accessing the game files of your legally purchased copy is the biggest hurdle in the process. Playing Bloodborne at acceptable framerates and resolutions on a modern system should not be so needlessly challenging and potentially DMCA-infringing, but it's difficult to imagine the situation improving in the near future.

Sony has largely turned its back on PC gaming after a brief, early 2020s dalliance, and it also recently put down remaster studio Bluepoint for no good reason. While that has spared us from anything like the Demon's Souls Remake being inflicted on Bloodborne, the commonsense, light touch PC port it should have received at any point in the last decade has never felt further away—even though Miyazaki himself told us he isn't against the idea.

title: The best Valheim mods for no-nonsense crafting, portable building plans, and more RNG sightseeing
author: Andrea Shearon
text:
It wasn't a long wait for some of my favorite Valheim mods to start working again after the 1.0 launch, and just as I expected, there were plenty of new fan-made features to tinker with. I'm still digging through the sea of new creations, but here's a list of some of the best Valheim mods I've found so far—along with advice on your mod manager options.
Valheim mod managers and required mods
Gale Mod Manager or R2ModMan
"Which mod manager do I use?" is an eternal dilemma, but I've been using Gale to mod Valheim since it works with both Thunderstore and Hexium downloads. If you're already using Thunderstore and don't feel like swapping, that should be just fine for the one site, but I like that Gale is lightweight with extended compatibility.
Gale Mod Manager | GitHub | Thunderstore
R2ModMan | GitHub | Thunderstore
Required Valheim mods
Most Valheim mods require BepInEx, while a ton of others require Jotunn, so you'll absolutely need the first while the second is negotiable. I recommend installing both, then launching Valheim before adding more mods into the mix. This way you can get troubleshooting the basics out of the way—you know, those modding best practices we all totally follow. Download one, launch, and test.
BepInExPack for Valheim | GitHub | Thunderstore Must be installed first
Drag and drop everything inside BepInExPack_Valheim into your Valheim directory
Example:
C:\SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Valheim
Jotunn | GitHub | Thunderstore | Nexus Install after BepInEx
Extract to your BepInEx plugins folder inside the same directory
Example: C:\SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Valheim\BepInEx\plugins\Jotunn
Best gameplay mods
by Grantapher
ValheimPlus (Fork)
You could slot this under any category, so I'll just kick the list off with Valheim Plus. It's packed with options available as individual mods—some of which are covered in the list below—but most are toggleable if you don't like the effect. Returning modders may be a little confused by Grantapher's spin-off, but this is a community-sourced fix after the original modder stopped publishing updates, and widely accepted as the replacement mod.
📥 Github | Thunderstore | Nexus | Hexium
by Warpalicious
More World Locations AIO
While I love Valheim's randomized terrain and sporadic ruins, I do wish we had a little more variety sprinkled throughout the decay. This mod from Warpalicious goes above and beyond my most basic ask and adds a ton of goodies, including 188 custom locations, shipping ports, more NPCs, and random shrines that bestow buffs.
📥 GitHub | Thunderstore
by DeathMonger
TheGreatestPortal
At first I loved the extra building task, but I've grown sick of making dedicated portal spaces that take up half my base. That's where The Greatest Portal mod comes in, and it's true to its name. Instead of building dozens of portals all over your base, you just need the one that provides a list of portals you've built all over the world.
📥 GitHub | Thunderstore | Hexium
by Advize
PlantEverything
I've always wanted to plant things like berry bushes and mushrooms in Valheim, and Advize's mod answers my prayers by adding those options to the cultivator. I don't even care about the impact it may have on resource balance. I just want a cute little bush by my garden for the vibes.
📥 GitHub | Thunderstore | Nexus
Best building and furniture mods
by Advize
PlantEasily
I can't keep plants alive in real life, and I'm no better at it when playing Vikings. PlantEasily keeps me from killing my Valheim crops by providing a grid for perfect planting distance between veggies. I also love the option for random rotation that prevents my fields from developing that uncanny symmetry look. Ick.
📥 Thunderstore | Nexus Mods
by Mathias Decrock
PlanBuild
This is hands down my favorite Valheim mod, and I'm relieved to see it well maintained and updated after 1.0. PlanBuild lets you construct base build blueprints without using any of the materials—blueprints that you can save, relocate, and build later.
📥 GitHub | Thunderstore | Nexus
by TastyChickenLegs
Floors Stairs Ladders Are Roofs
I already used stairs and ladders as decorative roof pieces, but dreaded having to repair the ones left exposed to rain. This tweak eliminates the need to climb onto the roof and fix everything taking water damage.
📥 Thunderstore | Nexus
by OdinPlus
OdinsFoodBarrels
I don't go for a ton of custom furniture in Valheim, but I love these decorative barrels that make my Viking kitchens feel a little more distinct from the rest of my base build. Bonus points for being functional. I just wanted them as decor, but it's nice to see they actually work.
📥 Thunderstore | Hexium
Best quality-of-life mods
by Azumatt
AzuCraftyBoxes
One of my biggest gripes with Valheim is that you still can't craft directly from chests in vanilla. What I like most about Azumatt's mod solution is its ability to configure finer details, so I can limit certain items and not accidentally waste rare resources.
📥 Thunderstore | Hexium
by Goldenrevolver
Quick Stack Store Restock
Valheim's quick stack is rather clunky, and I accidentally open and close chests while trying to merge hauls. This mod circumvents the messy vanilla process with one simple button for different commands like quick stack, restock, store all, and more.
📥 Thunderstore | Nexus Mods
by Morda
Workbenches+
I appreciate Valheim's build menu update in the 1.0 launch, but the crafting benches remain a mess. Workbenches Plus adds categories, an option to sort and filter, and keeps everything in order by biome.
📥 GitHub | Thunderstore | Nexus
by MSchmoecker
MultiUserChest
There's nothing more irritating than waiting in line for access to a chest, especially when multiple Vikings want a chance to dig through it. This mod reduces my urge to utter a passive-aggressive "are you done yet?" since multiple people can access one chest at a time.
📥 GitHub | Thunderstore
Best visual tools and texture mods
by Azumatt
Build Camera
I love building in first person and taking scenic screenshots, but that becomes a chore after toggling console commands on and off a few times. Azumatt's camera mod is 1.0-ready, and after just a few sessions of doing things the good ol' fashioned way, I'm more thankful for it than ever.
📥 GitHub | Hexium
by ChampandChris
Enhanced Lighting
Vanilla Valheim's lighting is gorgeous, but this mod offers more control and brightens areas that were once lost to darkness. I may actually know what the Swamp looks like now, and honestly, it's worth it for that alone.
📥 Nexus
by MommaMuffin
Valhalla ReShade HD
It's not often I find a ReShade preset that satisfies me right out of the box, but this one looks fantastic. If you're using a mod manager, you'll need to install ReShade ( official site ) separately, but I swear it's worth it for the visual flair. It's also a toy you can take to other games, and probably my first go-to tweak when modding anything.
📥 Nexus
Valheim biomes : Follow along zone by zone
Valheim console commands : Godly shortcuts
Valheim inventory upgrades : Deeper pockets
Valheim battle idols : Upgrade your gear
Valheim Grappling Hook : Mistlands made easy
Valheim Intricate Key : A key to the endgame

title: 8 strong Elder Scrolls opinions: With over 2,500 combined hours (and not all as stealth archers), we shout at each other about Skyrim, Morrowind, and Oblivion
author: Christopher Livingston
text:
We've become the Nerevarine and defeated Dagoth Ur. We've foiled Mehrunes Dagon and closed the Oblivion gates. We've destroyed Alduin and absorbed his soul. We've bought horse armor, stolen an Elder Scroll, and even once pickpocked a note from the butt of a fully-dressed assassin without him noticing .
In other words, we've done it all, and with a combined 2,500+ hours across the series, five PC Gamer editors have come together to say few things about the past and future of The Elder Scrolls series.
Below, we've shouted some of our strongest opinions about TES—and don't worry, Dragonborn, we've left some room for you to Fus-Ro-Dah yourself. After each opinion, you can click a button to tell us if you agree or disagree with our scalding hot takes.
The Elder Scrolls should be an RPG again
(Image credit: Bethesda) What gets Todd Howard out of bed every morning is the possibility of removing yet more numbers from Tamriel. Stats? Delete them. Skill points? Crush them. You want to play a distinct class , you sick freak? Absolutely not. Please hand yourself into the authorities.
But what this has done is turned the general experience of playing a Bethesda game into a uniform mush . Not in the sense that we're all stealth archers now (though that is a problem), but in the sense that, play any of these games for long enough and you simply become a master of everything. A lack of limitations, a willingness to tell a player they can't do something, that this or that skill is simply outside their remit, has made Bethesda's games more accessible but also more boring. It's time to go back to the old ways .
Skyrim's main quest is better than most of its sidequests
(Image credit: Bethesda) There was an intense contrast between how fun Oblivion's Thieves Guild, Dark Brotherhood, and Daedric Prince sidequests were and how boring its main questline was. Even the Fighter's Guild had some twists. I think that experience must have traumatized a generation of players, because I can't think of any other reason why people say the same thing about Skyrim.
In Skyrim, the Thieves Guild are a pack of losers and to get anywhere with their story you have to level them up by doing procedurally generated filler jobs. The Dark Brotherhood quests have little of the Hitman flair of Oblivion's, and mostly just end with you killing targets the same way you'd murder a bandit. Rare highlights like A Night to Remember aside, Skyrim's sidequests are nothing special.
But its main quest has you fighting dragons, climbing mountains, and travelling to the land of the dead . It's full of spectacle and also Paarthurnax, one of the few memorable NPCs in the entire game. Best of all, it doesn't demand you run a single Oblivion Gate.
Oblivion's spellmaking should've never gone away
(Image credit: Bethesda) Look, I know that Oblivion's spellmaking feature—wherein you could create your own custom spells—completely broke the game. It was possible to make absolutely absurd combinations of abilities that'd render a sufficiently-talented mage effectively immortal. As such, I'm not entirely surprised such a feature wasn't in Skyrim.
However: As Josh correctly identified above, TES has been less of an RPG with every installment anyway. And more to the point, I don't think it's ever been a particularly engaging RPG in recent years. This isn't Diablo, it's not Baldur's Gate—the amount of min-maxing you can do usually involves picking what type of armor you'd like to wear and a weapon, and that's pretty much it.
There's no real grist or art to making a strong Elder Scrolls character anyway, so why not let us have fun breaking the game over our knee? More to the point, the idea of a wizard starting out as a little weenie, then achieving godlike power? That's pure oldschool D&D, baby, and Oblivion's spellmaking was delightfully flavourful for that exact reason.
Morrowind is great, but they didn't know how to do side quests yet
(Image credit: Bethesda) When you're a Serious Critic who loves RPGs, you're required by law to say that Morrowind is the best Elder Scrolls game⁠—I might even agree still, grousing aside⁠—but I feel like Oblivion and Skyrim do not get their proper due for the leaps they made in side quest design.
Morrowind's final Thieves Guild mission is a straightforward assassination of some Nord guy . Oblivion's is the stone cold classic, first round hall of famer, The Ultimate Heist , a multipart infiltration where you steal an Elder Scroll from the Imperial Palace. There are twists and funny moments in Morrowind's side content, but nothing as shocking as A Night to Remember in Skyrim .
Morrowind's atmosphere, worldbuilding, and main quest are still some of Bethesda's finest, and I'm pretty reliably the person who prefers a crusty old RPG to the new hotness. But it always bugs me that people (mostly RPG Codex guys and YouTubers) are always in such a rush to not be seen liking the popular thing that they miss the nuances of what they're criticizing.
I don't think current-day Bethesda has another good Dark Brotherhood questline in 'em
(Image credit: Bethesda) The Dark Brotherhood questline from Oblivion is generally regarded as one of the best—and for good reason. Not only is the story pretty stellar, but "Whodunnit?" is a stand-out in that it's a genuinely impressive spiderweb of potential outcomes. The Summitmist Manor is almost like a miniature immersive sim. Obviously not as complex, sure, but a delicious bite-sized playground in which to murder its guests.
But after Starfield? Man, I don't know. No questline I played in that deeply beige game had any of that same Dark Brotherhood juice. And given what we've heard out of the studio—namely, tighter and tighter constraints on what its developers can do— I'm not sure that the magic's there for a good Brotherhood questline anymore .
I'd like to be wrong, but in my mind? A Dark Brotherhood questline requires more weirdness, creativity, and gallows humour than modern-day Bethesda seems capable of.
Bethesda should ditch handwritten stories and turn TES into first-person Dwarf Fortress
(Image credit: Bethesda) Bethesda's writing took a dip in Oblivion and has been generally anodyne since Skyrim (the studio tried for something more interesting with Fallout 4—and I genuinely admire it for doing so—but it didn't work out), with Starfield's bland, sexless galaxy providing the absolute nadir of its narrative efforts so far. You might say the answer is to change how it approaches writing its games. I say no.
Bethesda has flirted with emergent, systems-driven gameplay since Oblivion, but it's never truly committed. NPC schedules and relationship values are garnish on a stubbornly hand-crafted meal. It doesn't have to be that way, though. Go all in, guys. Do what you're best at, which is creating rich, wide worlds to explore, then fill it with mechanics and systems that drive the action rather than your half-baked plots . You know, like Mount & Blade. You guys should just make Mount & Blade.
I don't care if I have to pass through a loading screen for interiors as long as I can still pick up garbage and wave it around
(Image credit: Bethesda) Cyberpunk 2077 may be one of my favorite RPGs ever, but do you remember its inventory screen? It feels so videogamey, so disconnected from the world you're exploring. What about clutter in that world, its interactivity? All those drinks and snacks you can pick up are fairly static objects, no fun physics interactions, no soul .
The fact that you can just wander into somebody's house in The Elder Scrolls and read the books on their shelves, drag their dinner off the table, rearrange their cutlery, it has such a profound pound-for-pound effect on the games' immersion . Other games have managed a similar magic⁠—Baldur's Gate 3, Deus Ex, Prey⁠—but nobody does it in an open world simulation like Bethesda can. These granular, interactive environments are truly something special.
So I say let TES6 get diced up into a billion discrete loading zones . That's not the problem I had with Starfield, and if it's somehow required for the interactive environments I've loved from this studio, it's a price I'll gladly pay.
It's ridiculous there's not an Elder Scrolls TV show on right now
(Image credit: Bethesda) I don't get Bethesda sometimes. They have a massively popular Fallout TV series yet they don't fast-track a new Fallout game (until they're forced to by Microsoft), and they have a massively popular Elder Scrolls game series and don't get a TES television show into production (as far as we know). All the ingredients to cross-polinate are there. Just, like… do it?

I'm sure every TV executive would stare blankly at nerdy writers pitching a show about the devastating death toll and political consequences of the Thrassian Plague before saying "But we still have a guy in a horned helmet shouting at dragons, right?" But, c'mon, Bethesda. You announced The Elder Scrolls 6: Subtitle Pending 35 years ago (it feels like), at least give us some TES to watch while we wait for more TES to play .

We've become the Nerevarine and defeated Dagoth Ur. We've foiled Mehrunes Dagon and closed the Oblivion gates. We've destroyed Alduin and absorbed his soul. We've bought horse armor, stolen an Elder Scroll, and even once pickpocked a note from the butt of a fully-dressed assassin without him noticing.

In other words, we've done it all, and with a combined 2,500+ hours across the series, five PC Gamer editors have come together to say few things about the past and future of The Elder Scrolls series.

Below, we've shouted some of our strongest opinions about TES—and don't worry, Dragonborn, we've left some room for you to Fus-Ro-Dah yourself. After each opinion, you can click a button to tell us if you agree or disagree with our scalding hot takes.

The Elder Scrolls should be an RPG again

What gets Todd Howard out of bed every morning is the possibility of removing yet more numbers from Tamriel. Stats? Delete them. Skill points? Crush them. You want to play a distinct class, you sick freak? Absolutely not. Please hand yourself into the authorities.

But what this has done is turned the general experience of playing a Bethesda game into a uniform mush. Not in the sense that we're all stealth archers now (though that is a problem), but in the sense that, play any of these games for long enough and you simply become a master of everything. A lack of limitations, a willingness to tell a player they can't do something, that this or that skill is simply outside their remit, has made Bethesda's games more accessible but also more boring. It's time to go back to the old ways.

Skyrim's main quest is better than most of its sidequests

There was an intense contrast between how fun Oblivion's Thieves Guild, Dark Brotherhood, and Daedric Prince sidequests were and how boring its main questline was. Even the Fighter's Guild had some twists. I think that experience must have traumatized a generation of players, because I can't think of any other reason why people say the same thing about Skyrim.

In Skyrim, the Thieves Guild are a pack of losers and to get anywhere with their story you have to level them up by doing procedurally generated filler jobs. The Dark Brotherhood quests have little of the Hitman flair of Oblivion's, and mostly just end with you killing targets the same way you'd murder a bandit. Rare highlights like A Night to Remember aside, Skyrim's sidequests are nothing special.

But its main quest has you fighting dragons, climbing mountains, and travelling to the land of the dead. It's full of spectacle and also Paarthurnax, one of the few memorable NPCs in the entire game. Best of all, it doesn't demand you run a single Oblivion Gate.

Oblivion's spellmaking should've never gone away

Look, I know that Oblivion's spellmaking feature—wherein you could create your own custom spells—completely broke the game. It was possible to make absolutely absurd combinations of abilities that'd render a sufficiently-talented mage effectively immortal. As such, I'm not entirely surprised such a feature wasn't in Skyrim.

However: As Josh correctly identified above, TES has been less of an RPG with every installment anyway. And more to the point, I don't think it's ever been a particularly engaging RPG in recent years. This isn't Diablo, it's not Baldur's Gate—the amount of min-maxing you can do usually involves picking what type of armor you'd like to wear and a weapon, and that's pretty much it.

There's no real grist or art to making a strong Elder Scrolls character anyway, so why not let us have fun breaking the game over our knee? More to the point, the idea of a wizard starting out as a little weenie, then achieving godlike power? That's pure oldschool D&D, baby, and Oblivion's spellmaking was delightfully flavourful for that exact reason.

Morrowind is great, but they didn't know how to do side quests yet

When you're a Serious Critic who loves RPGs, you're required by law to say that Morrowind is the best Elder Scrolls game⁠—I might even agree still, grousing aside⁠—but I feel like Oblivion and Skyrim do not get their proper due for the leaps they made in side quest design.

Morrowind's final Thieves Guild mission is a straightforward assassination of some Nord guy. Oblivion's is the stone cold classic, first round hall of famer, The Ultimate Heist, a multipart infiltration where you steal an Elder Scroll from the Imperial Palace. There are twists and funny moments in Morrowind's side content, but nothing as shocking as A Night to Remember in Skyrim.

Morrowind's atmosphere, worldbuilding, and main quest are still some of Bethesda's finest, and I'm pretty reliably the person who prefers a crusty old RPG to the new hotness. But it always bugs me that people (mostly RPG Codex guys and YouTubers) are always in such a rush to not be seen liking the popular thing that they miss the nuances of what they're criticizing.

I don't think current-day Bethesda has another good Dark Brotherhood questline in 'em

The Dark Brotherhood questline from Oblivion is generally regarded as one of the best—and for good reason. Not only is the story pretty stellar, but "Whodunnit?" is a stand-out in that it's a genuinely impressive spiderweb of potential outcomes. The Summitmist Manor is almost like a miniature immersive sim. Obviously not as complex, sure, but a delicious bite-sized playground in which to murder its guests.

But after Starfield? Man, I don't know. No questline I played in that deeply beige game had any of that same Dark Brotherhood juice. And given what we've heard out of the studio—namely, tighter and tighter constraints on what its developers can do—I'm not sure that the magic's there for a good Brotherhood questline anymore.

I'd like to be wrong, but in my mind? A Dark Brotherhood questline requires more weirdness, creativity, and gallows humour than modern-day Bethesda seems capable of.

Bethesda should ditch handwritten stories and turn TES into first-person Dwarf Fortress

Bethesda's writing took a dip in Oblivion and has been generally anodyne since Skyrim (the studio tried for something more interesting with Fallout 4—and I genuinely admire it for doing so—but it didn't work out), with Starfield's bland, sexless galaxy providing the absolute nadir of its narrative efforts so far. You might say the answer is to change how it approaches writing its games. I say no.

Bethesda has flirted with emergent, systems-driven gameplay since Oblivion, but it's never truly committed. NPC schedules and relationship values are garnish on a stubbornly hand-crafted meal. It doesn't have to be that way, though. Go all in, guys. Do what you're best at, which is creating rich, wide worlds to explore, then fill it with mechanics and systems that drive the action rather than your half-baked plots. You know, like Mount & Blade. You guys should just make Mount & Blade.

I don't care if I have to pass through a loading screen for interiors as long as I can still pick up garbage and wave it around

Cyberpunk 2077 may be one of my favorite RPGs ever, but do you remember its inventory screen? It feels so videogamey, so disconnected from the world you're exploring. What about clutter in that world, its interactivity? All those drinks and snacks you can pick up are fairly static objects, no fun physics interactions, no soul.

The fact that you can just wander into somebody's house in The Elder Scrolls and read the books on their shelves, drag their dinner off the table, rearrange their cutlery, it has such a profound pound-for-pound effect on the games' immersion. title: Call of Duty 'cosmetic toggle' will cleanse Warzone of its Party City aesthetic
author: Morgan Park
text:
Warzone is trying something new
In Warzone, a "cosmetic toggle" that will disable legacy character skins at a client level
With this toggle, players will instead see operators from Modern Warfare 4, making the game stylistically cohesive
This toggle only exists within Warzone, as Modern Warfare 4 itself won't carry forward any cosmetics from past games.
This time last year, Call of Duty had to look itself in the mirror and admit that all the ugly crossover skins had gotten out of hand. The company committed to a clean break with Black Ops 7: No old skins would carry forward, and future cosmetics would have to fit the Black Ops universe to make the cut. That lasted for about three months, when a CoD x Fallout collaboration arrived and all bets were off again.
This new toggle is, without a doubt, a positive change for CoD that I personally never expected to happen. If I were a Warzone diehard, I'd turn this on from day one and never look back. It's a shame, though, that this toggle appears to be only a temporary vacation from tacky outfits.
Since, according to this blog post , skins from Modern Warfare 4 aren't filtered out with the toggle, Warzone players will still be subject to whatever future attire is destined for the new game. So Warzone will only be stylistically cohesive for as long as Modern Warfare 4 is. By the time Season 6 rolls around, we might have Timothée Chalamet in Dune gear or Travis Kelce running amok in Warzone, and the toggle would be rendered pointless.
That is, unless Infinity Ward makes its own commitment to non-goofy cosmetics between now and launch, or expands the toggle to exclude all store outfits. I've reached out to Activision for clarification on how this will work.

title: Experimental RPG developer Summer Eternal: 'We're giving away 5% of our studio to you, the Players' in order to 'mend the trust broken in this industry a thousand times over'
author: Ted Litchfield
text:
Summer Eternal is an RPG studio co-founded by ex-ZA/UM designers Argo Tuulik and Dora Klindžić, as well as developer/organizer Aleksandar Gavrilović (quoted above). Given the former two developers' experience working on a canceled Disco Elysium expansion , it makes sense they'd want to try something radically different for their new studio's financing and governance.
Worker-owned cooperatives are rare but not unheard-of in games, but Summer Eternal is also looking to offer ownership stakes (and profit sharing) to its freelancers and customers. Crucially, it's not in the form of "walkin' around money" for the latter group. Instead, Summer Eternal wants to offer players a democratic say in the studio's direction, backed up by control of 5% of the profits.
It reminds me of the EVE Online Council of Stellar Management or Old School RuneScape's player voting on new features, but with this added element of the studio literally putting its money where its mouth is. At a time when traditionally governed, publicly-traded games companies are cannibalizing themselves before our eyes to fulfil a fiduciary duty to their shareholders, such an economically and politically radical proposition might have more broad appeal than it used to.
You can read Gavrilović's full posts on the governance of Summer Eternal and the profit-directing player non-profit on the studio's website. If you'd like to get in on the ground floor as a player-stakeholder, Summer Eternal's first product is actually a book.
The Summer Eternal Anthology Vol. 1 is one-half a collection of essays on the state of games and the industry, with guest writers and interviewees including the likes of Dragon Age scribe David Gaider and former Greek finance minister and Valve economist, Yanis Varoufakis.
The other half is a design document previewing and formally announcing Summer Eternal's first game, Project Red Rooster. At the time of writing, the Anthology is available for preorder for one more day.

title: 14 days in Dragon Shelter: A play by play of my first season in the Stardew-style farm sim where dragons help bake pies
author: Lauren Morton
text:
Day 1: Anybody home?
(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio) I arrive at my grandpa's overgrown old cottage alone. Where's he run off to? Apparently I don't know. There's only enough time on day one to read several tutorial popups telling me what to do next (oh dear, that ta-dah noise is going to get on my nerves fast), cut a few trees with my axe so I can use wood to fix my bed, and go to sleep.
Day 2: There's always free seeds
Today I get to walk into town and oh, jeez, everyone here is Eeyore-level sad, heads facing navels and all. Even the music is depressing. The mayor tells me the town's in shambles and everyone's gone away and maybe I could help the couple folks who are left.
Well then, it's time to roll up my farm simming sleeves. The merchant wants berries which I can pick a ton of growing wild on my farm. The carpenter wants me to fix a cart by chopping wood. The gardener wants me to try growing wheat on my farm. Done, done, and done!
In the midst of doing all that though, I'm surprised by which things Dragon Shelter considers worthy of popup explainers versus what goes completely unexplained without even an indicator in the interface. Basic things like navigating my backpack are very fiddly and there's a "tips" button to find out which season seeds grow in before I buy them—important information that's available as a tooltip if you use keyboard and mouse but requires the unmentioned button press if you use a game pad, which Dragon Shelter recommends.
The tool animations and movement aren't clunky though, so that's one for the pros and one for the cons column on my normal gripes with 3D farm sims.
By about 8 pm I've acquired a shovel, watering can, pickaxe, wheat seeds, and a blueprint for an outdoor kitchen. I don't have the time or enough energy meter left to clear a spot on my property for it, so off to bed I go.
Day 3: Time for a jam session
(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio) I spend all morning clear cutting a large section of my yard to plop my outdoor kitchen onto. It comes pre-equipped with an oven, cauldron, matches, and a couple other basics so I can make some berry jam for the mayor.
The menu for queuing up recipes to cook is, like all the others, awkward and shabby-looking. I'm a bit of a snob about interface designs, sorry. It's just a shame the environments in Dragon Shelter are so cute and the menus don't match at all. In fact, what happened to the nicer-looking HUD that's in some of its Steam store page screenshots?
The tools bar in Dragon Shelter's earlier store page screenshots. Wild Forest Studio The HUD in Dragon Shelter at launch. Wild Forest Studio The cooking system is easy enough to understand, though. A list of visual steps for the recipe I've queued appears in the top left when I step into my kitchen:
Take berries from the basket
Put them in the fruit press and hit a button several times to mash
Pick up the cauldron and carry it over to add berries, water, and sugar
Place it on the fire
Grab logs for fuel
Etc, and so forth
It doesn't have the "oh god the food is burning!" hustle of something like Overcooked or the minigame-ification of each step like Palia, but I can see the promise.
Day 4: Cursed kitchen reno
(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio) What the heck? How do I add new cooking stations to my kitchen? Why is this not something that had a little ta-dah popup to explain it to me? I've been standing here half the in-game day confused.
Oh, I can't add stations while a recipe is queued up. There's nothing indicating that as the problem, but it's tucked into the "cooking" portion of the help menu. I would cook a berry pie for my current quest but my wheat isn't finished growing. Fine, I'll go to bed early!
Day 5: Dragon!
Finally I meet a dragon today! The liquid-y critter crawls out of the pond next to my house when it smells the berry pie I'm cooking. I feed it raw berries and we're best friends immediately. It doesn't seem like I can give it a name though. It's just "water dragon," bummer.
Cooking with my dragon friend is quite cute. It will try to do the next step in whichever recipe is queued up, like adding water (from its mouth, aww) to a cauldron for berry jam while I go grab another set of berries to mash for the next jar of jam in the queue. There are moments it gets a little confused if I'm working too fast for my dragon to pick up a step. It seems to work best if I start the process but then let my dragon finish a recipe while I jump ahead to begin the next dish so we don't step on each others' toes.
Day 6 - 9: How to train my pet dragon
I spend my first few days with my dragon pal growing wheat and potatoes, chopping wood on my farm, and cooking bread together. My dragon will automatically help with what obviously needs doing like watering crops right when we wake up. I can also queue up chores for it like chopping trees or rocks if I equip it with tools.
The carpenter offers to make me a trampoline for my dragon to enjoy and, boy howdy, if you thought cows playing with beach balls was cute in Fields of Mistria you're going to love a dragon bouncing on a trampoline.
On day nine the mayor tells me to start earning the trust of all the townsfolk with gifts and quests and I can use the "request board" to deliver them recipes they want like baked potatoes or bread.
Day 10: Standard farm simming routines
Alright, the "just one more chore" feeling of a farm sim has finally kicked in. Here's my day:
Water my crops
Collect sticks and hay to help the merchant fix his stall
Cook 4x baked potatoes with my dragon
Deliver one baked potato to the merchant so he'll fix his store
Deliver the other baked potato to the gardener to earn some friendship points
Feed two baked potatoes to my dragon because it's hungry
Sell produce so I can buy nails from the merchant to give to the blacksmith for a quest
I'm only just now noticing that there doesn't seem to be a map. Which is making it tricky to remember where to turn in quests. The bigger issue is how small the world feels. I've been just running back and forth between two areas: my farm property and the tiny town. Is there more to the world? I can't tell.
Day 11-13: The chores continue
In week two my chores continue: The mayor needs me to bring clay and hay to repair a dovecote so the village can have contact with the world outside again. The new rancher needs the watering dish fixed for his giant insect-looking critter. I've got to buy more nails from the merchant to fix the pier and I'm getting a bit suspicious of all the excuses the blacksmith has for why he can't just make nails himself.
I've welcomed a new alchemist, a weaver, a fisherman, and a bard to town. So many folks have come back but they're all still comically sad. The mayor proposes I cook food for a village festival, so maybe that will help the mood around here.
Day 14: It's very cute, but…
(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio) Dragon Shelter goes for the 14 day season instead of 28, so I've already made it to the end of spring. It seems that I'll be adding more stations to my kitchen to expand the recipes I can take on, but there don't appear to be a bunch of other crafting type stations that I'm going to plop on my property to create goods. I should unlock animal tending on my farm soon (aside from my dragon) so I'm eager to see that part too.
It's a cute game, but much smaller than I'd expected, so far. Shops don't have interiors (yet?) so I just talk with the owners outside. The villagers themselves really just deliver quests and don't have memorable personalities. If there's more to the world than just the two areas, I've no way to know yet. Its store page references "a vibrant fantasy world filled with magical biomes," but I can't tell when those other areas might appear.
From what I've seen so far, Dragon Shelter leans mostly on the novelty of doing chores alongside my dragons and the increasing demands of the cooking minigame as I add more stations. It doesn't seem likely to deliver a detailed story or intense profit min-maxxing of some other farm sims. It's just dragons and vibes, but they are good vibes.
